figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: GaussianRenderFormer renders 3D Gaussian splats with a neural network, without a rasterizer. Top: the reference, a rasterization of each object’s full splat. Bottom (ours): GaussianRenderFormer from a 20,000-Gaussian input, on six objects never seen in training, chosen by hand for variety. Right: a $3\times$ zoom of the most detailed region of the last object, where the model softens the stone’s texture.
figures.headline: The model renders six unseen objects from 20,000-Gaussian inputs without a rasterizer, shown beside full-splat references.
citing_sentences: Given a set of Gaussians and a camera, our model outputs the image directly, without per-scene optimization and with no rasterizer in the renderer (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of GaussianRenderFormer. Each Gaussian’s 14 parameters are embedded as one token, and a view-independent scene encoder (top) lets these tokens exchange information, using a 3D rotary embedding of their centers. For each view, the image is split into $4\times 4$-pixel patches, and each patch becomes a token built from its camera rays. The view decoder (bottom) lets these tokens attend to the scene tokens, using a 2D rotary embedding of where each Gaussian lands in the image and an embedding of its projected footprint, and a DPT head turns them into pixels.
figures.headline: Each Gaussian becomes one token, a scene encoder mixes the tokens, and a view decoder turns patch tokens into pixels.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Three fresh held-out objects, chosen at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of GaussianRenderFormer’s per-object PSNR. From left to right: the reference (the full, unpruned splat rasterized with gsplat), gsplat on the pruned 20,000-Gaussian input, GaussianRenderFormer on the same input, and the absolute error of each against the reference, scaled by 5. GaussianRenderFormer scores 34.5, 39.5 and 41.7 dB on these views, and gsplat on the input 39.7, 45.5 and 45.7 dB. GaussianRenderFormer gets shapes and colors right, and its error concentrates on edges and fine texture.
figures.headline: On held-out objects at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, the model scores 34.5, 39.5 and 41.7 dB, with errors on edges and texture.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows three held-out objects, at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of the model’s score.
Figure 9 shows the harness arms and the full-scale models of Section 6.2 on objects of Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: PSNR against the unpruned render when the end of stage 2, which has seen all 26,820 objects, is fine-tuned on fewer objects, with the same number of steps for every point. With one object the model fits its training images and forgets the others. The two curves meet at the full set, far below rasterizing the same input. The triangles show the final model, trained about 10 times longer with the footprint.
figures.headline: Fine-tuning on one object makes the model forget others, and even the full set stays far below rasterizing the same input.
citing_sentences: To see how much the amount of data matters, we fine-tune the end of stage 2 with the recipe of the harness (Section 6.2), before the footprint was added, on 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 objects and on all 26,820, with the same number of steps (Figure 4).

figures.caption: The arms of Table 4 and the full-scale models on the first and third objects of Figure 3: the first object (top), and $4\times$ close-ups of the region of each of the two objects with the most detail (middle and bottom). The final model keeps the painted pattern of the first object, and the same recipe trained without the footprint renders it slightly softer. The models of the 1,000-object harness, trained for about a tenth as long, are softer, and lose much of the pattern without the footprint, without the 2D embedding and with $8\times 8$ patches. figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Failure cases. The four fresh held-out objects with the lowest mean PSNR of GaussianRenderFormer, each at its worst view. Columns as in Figure 3, with errors scaled by 5. GaussianRenderFormer scores 25.4, 27.2, 29.1 and 28.5 dB on these views, and gsplat on the input 37.9, 40.0, 38.6 and 40.4 dB. The shapes are right on all four. The error comes from dense texture that GaussianRenderFormer renders less precisely than the reference (the clouds on the globe, the facade of the building, the houses and trees of the town) and from soft, low-contrast structure (the streaks on the ground under the sign).

abstract: Can a neural network learn to render 3D Gaussian splats on its own, with no rasterizer in the renderer? We present GaussianRenderFormer, a transformer that takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Each Gaussian becomes one token in a view-independent encoder, and a view-dependent decoder turns small patches of camera rays into pixels by attending to those tokens. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, GaussianRenderFormer renders 300 unseen objects at 38.08 dB PSNR against the full, unpruned splats, while rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The gap is not one of generalization, and our diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder: telling it the projected footprint of each Gaussian, which it could in principle infer, adds 1.4 dB. Under-training is not ruled out. Code, trained models and videos: https://svlwoof.github.io/gaussianrenderformer.

sections.body: The introduction motivates a learned renderer for Gaussian splats. Current methods render them only with hand-written rasterizers. RenderFormer does this for triangle meshes, but to the authors' knowledge no learned renderer existed for Gaussians. The paper proposes GaussianRenderFormer, which takes a set of Gaussians and a camera and outputs the image directly. Trained on 26,820 Objaverse objects pruned to 20,000 Gaussians each, it reaches 38.08 dB against the full splats on 300 unseen objects. Rasterizing the same pruned input reaches 44.02 dB. The authors call this a feasibility study at the object level, and they state that under-training is not ruled out.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: No learned renderer for 3D Gaussian splats existed, so this paper tests whether a transformer can output images directly.

sections.body: Related work falls into four groups. Rendering 3D Gaussians uses hand-written rasterizers and ray tracers, which the authors compare against. Learned renderers for explicit scenes include RenderFormer and its successors for meshes, RenderNet for voxel grids, and transformers that render point clouds. Networks around Gaussian splatting mostly produce Gaussians from images or use them as tokens for other tasks, and then rasterize them. View-synthesis transformers such as LVSM decode pixels from ray queries, but they take posed images rather than explicit Gaussians. The authors state that, to their knowledge, none of these renders a given set of Gaussians with a network alone.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work renders Gaussians only with hand-written rasterizers, while learned renderers cover meshes, points or implicit scenes.

sections.body: This section gives the rasterization equation that the model replaces. A 3D Gaussian splat is a set of Gaussians, each with a center, covariance, opacity and color. A rasterizer projects each Gaussian to 2D, sorts them by depth and alpha-blends them front to back at each pixel. The paper uses only the view-independent color, a single RGB value. It then summarizes RenderFormer. Each triangle becomes one token in a view-independent stage with 12 self-attention layers and 16 register tokens. Each 8×8-pixel patch becomes a token in a view-dependent stage with six cross-attention layers and a DPT head. RenderFormer is trained on scenes of up to 4,096 triangles.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: The rasterizer that GaussianRenderFormer replaces projects, sorts and blends Gaussians, while RenderFormer renders meshes with two transformer stages.

sections.body: The model keeps RenderFormer's two-stage layout and pretrained weights, and changes the input and the view decoder. Each Gaussian's 14 numbers (center, scales, rotation quaternion, color and opacity) are embedded as one token. A view-independent encoder with 3D rotary embeddings lets the tokens exchange information. The view decoder uses 4×4-pixel patches and three changes. A 2D rotary embedding encodes where each Gaussian's center lands in the image. A projected footprint is added to the attention keys through zero-initialized layers. Smaller patches give the decoder four times as many tokens. The footprint is computed in closed form, so per-pixel visibility and blending are left to the network. Training runs in four stages, the last at 512 pixels with LPIPS.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Each Gaussian becomes one token, and the view decoder gets projected centers, footprints and four-by-four-pixel patches.

sections.body: The data come from `Objaverse_Splats`, a subset of ShapeSplat. The authors keep splats with a PSNR of at least 32 dB, an LPIPS of at most 0.06 and exactly 50,000 Gaussians, which leaves 26,820 training objects and 1,806 validation objects. Each object is centered, rotated so that its up axis is +y, and scaled so that its largest coordinate is 0.45. Ground truth is 28 gsplat renders of the full splat at 512×512 pixels with a 45° field of view. Inputs keep 20,000 Gaussians chosen by an importance score adapted from LightGaussian, then are fine-tuned for 1,500 steps against renders of the full splat from 64 views. The evaluation uses 300 development objects and 300 fresh objects, all held out from training.
sections.heading: Data
sections.headline: Training uses 26,820 Objaverse objects, each pruned to 20,000 Gaussians from splats of 50,000, with ground-truth renders.

sections.body: The main result is on 300 fresh held-out objects over all 28 views at three training distances. GaussianRenderFormer scores 38.08 dB against the unpruned render, and gsplat on the same pruned input scores 44.02 dB. The gap is 3.9 dB at distance 1.15 and 6.8 dB at 1.7. On training objects the model scores only 0.17 dB higher than on unseen objects, so the authors conclude the gap is not one of generalization. Rendering one view takes 275 ms on one L40S GPU, while gsplat takes under a millisecond. The footprint adds 1.4 dB at full scale, according to the ablation in Table 7.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 300 unseen objects the model scores 38.08 dB against the full splat, below the 44.02 dB of rasterizing the same pruned input.

sections.body: The authors list several limits. The model stays several dB below rasterizing the same input and is several hundred times slower with more memory. Its time and memory grow quickly with input size. It is trained and tested only on single objects viewed from outside, so rendering a full scene with the camera inside remains open. It renders well only in its training camera configuration. Other input sizes, distances, resolutions and fields of view cost it quality. It uses only view-independent color and cannot relight. Preparing inputs from larger splats still uses a rasterizer for pruning. Starting from RenderFormer's weights limits what can change, and training is expensive and depends on a pretrained mesh renderer.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: The model is several dB below rasterizing, hundreds of times slower, and limited to single objects in one camera configuration.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution. Starting from RenderFormer's weights, a token per Gaussian, a 2D rotary embedding, a projected footprint and smaller patches are enough for a network to render unseen objects in the training camera configuration. A clear gap to rasterizing the same input remains. The authors state that it is not a generalization gap, and that their diagnostics are consistent with a bottleneck in the view decoder, though under-training is not ruled out. They call a learned renderer for Gaussians feasible but not yet competitive. Future work follows the limitations, including giving each Gaussian material parameters and adding light sources to learn relighting and global illumination.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A network renders a given Gaussian set without a rasterizer, but the gap to rasterizing remains and the result is not yet competitive.

sections.body: Appendix A reports a 96-frame camera path, with 38.52 dB per frame for the model against 44.12 dB for gsplat on the input and a worst frame of 35.70 dB. Appendix B describes real captures of four Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, with their licensing notes and Table 6, which gives region PSNR at 20,000, 80,000 and 160,000 Gaussians. Appendix C gives supporting measurements, including the harness schedule, full-scale ablations, a reachable-target check, frozen-encoder fine-tuning, the camera configuration study and cost by input size. Appendix G gives reproducibility details: the released code and weights, stage durations and the settings of the final model in Table 16. A final part states the licenses.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists camera-path and real-capture results, supporting measurements, reproducibility settings, and licenses.
